item.title: ICE detainees allege excessive force during attempted removals to Mexico
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ICE detainees are asking a federal judge to intervene at the agency’s largest detention camp, citing sworn accounts alleging that guards beat people who resisted removal to Mexico and that masked personnel allegedly beat others and ordered them to cross the southern border. The motion for a preliminary injunction, filed Thursday in federal court in El Paso, Texas, concerns Camp East Montana, a sprawling immigration detention facility at Fort Bliss. The request is backed by declarations from 43 people, including current or former detainees and relatives or friends of those who died, 29 medical records, four government oversight reports and two expert declarations. Plaintiffs argue the conditions amount to unconstitutional punishment under the Fifth Amendment. One Cuban detainee claimed that guards slammed his head against a wall repeatedly and crushed his testicles after he refused removal to Mexico. Another detainee alleged they were taken toward the southern border, told to “jump over into Mexico,” and that masked personnel beat some who refused. A sign marks the entrance at the Camp East Montana immigrant detention center at a U.S. Army base, El Paso, Texas, February 13, 2026. The allegations have not been established by a court. The preliminary-injunction motion presents the plaintiffs’ evidence and arguments, and the judge has not ruled that the accusations are true. An ICE Office of Detention Oversight inspection found a 37.5 percent failure rate in February, including deficiencies involving use of force and restraints, security, sexual abuse and assault prevention, and tuberculosis protocols. Despite that, the inspection gave the facility an “Acceptable/Adequate” rating, according to the filing. An unannounced follow-up inspection in May found that overall deficiencies had increased from 49 to 52, while “Priority Component Deficiencies” rose from three to 12, according to the motion. Eight were repeat deficiencies. The report listed zero corrective actions, plaintiffs said. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has maintained that allegations concerning the conditions at Camp East Montana are “categorically false,” a “smear campaign” and “fearmongering clickbait.” Newsweek has contacted DHS and ICE for comment via email. Among the supporting evidence filed Thursday is a collection of declarations from detainees, many identified by pseudonyms. “Isaac,” a 43-year-old Cuban man, alleged guards confronted him in September 2025 after he refused removal to Mexico, returning with about 30 others. “Outside in the hallway, the guards started beating on me,” Isaac said in his sworn declaration. He said guards slammed his head against a wall about 10 times, twisted his ankles and crushed his testicles, leaving him with severe pain that lasted about a month. When they reached what Isaac understood to be the Mexican side of the border, he said approximately 15 to 20 masked people were there. A guard allegedly told the detainees that because their own countries would not accept them, Mexico was a good option, and that those who refused could instead be sent to “a jail cell in El Salvador or to Africa.” Isaac said he refused and was allowed back on the bus. He said only a Nicaraguan man and another Cuban man returned on the bus with him, while “the rest went to Mexico.” The exhibit also contains an anatomical diagram on which Isaac marked areas where he said guards injured him. Court documents contain an anatomical diagram on which Isaac marked areas where he said guards injured him. A second Cuban detainee, “Abel,” similarly alleged guards beat him after he refused to be cuffed and taken to Mexico. He said he was subsequently transported with about 13 others to the border near Santa Teresa, where masked people were present, and detainees were directed toward a bus bound for Mexico. Abel said only four people returned with him. Told to ‘Jump’ Into Mexico Another declaration, from a Cuban detainee identified as “Eduardo,” goes further. Eduardo alleged that on two occasions people working at the facility attempted to remove him to Mexico, despite his being Cuban and never having been there. He said that during one trip around October 23, 2025, he was transported with 10 Cubans and two Nicaraguans to Santa Teresa. The people who transported the group worked at the detention center, Eduardo said, while masked people were present near the border wall along with one unmasked ICE representative. “When the guards took us out of the truck, they replaced the metal cuffs with plastic ones and then told us to jump over into Mexico,” Eduardo said in the declaration. He alleged that detained people were warned they could face federal charges and remain in detention if they refused. “The masked people sometimes beat on people to get them to jump the wall even if they don’t want to,” Eduardo alleged. “I have seen other people get beaten up and forced to jump.” Eduardo said he refused to cross, although he claimed that “a lot of people” did. The filing does not identify the masked personnel Eduardo described, and his allegation does not by itself establish their agency or employer. The filings describe alleged beatings extending beyond the Mexico removals. “Eduardo” said guards beat him multiple times after he sought medication, including an October 2025 incident in which he alleged six or seven guards stomped on him while he was cuffed until he lost consciousness. He said another beating after his release from solitary left him bruised and bloody and required a second ambulance trip to a hospital. “Samuel,” a 19-year-old Venezuelan, alleged officers body-slammed and beat him after he turned off a light, breaking a tooth, crushing his testicles, and injuring his ear. He said he lost consciousness and was taken by ambulance to a hospital, and later reported continuing hearing loss and receiving a $1,140 medical bill related to the emergency visit. The preliminary-injunction motion alleges excessive force was systemic and cites ICE oversight findings that staff lacked training in de-escalation and use-of-force techniques and failed to document uses of force, preserve video and audio evidence, and conduct appropriate after-action reviews. The motion also cites a detainee death that the El Paso Medical Examiner ruled a homicide caused by”asphyxia due to neck and torso compression,” and says government oversight material found evidence connected to the death “was missing or destroyed.” Separately, plaintiffs allege guards fractured named plaintiff Gerald Akari Angye’s wrist and spine while he was shackled and not resisting. “Urgent protection is desperately needed at Camp East Montana,” Gerald Akari Angye said in a statement shared with Newsweek , alleging that detainees continue to lack adequate food, water, medicine and recreation. Angye said he would “never be the same” after the violence he alleges he experienced at the hands of guards. “The inhumane conditions at Camp East Montana seem to be getting worse. No one of good conscience can support what is happening there. I plead with the court to give relief to people held in the horrible Camp East Montana.” Plaintiffs also allege systemic medical failures involving access to medication and treatment for conditions including tuberculosis, cancer, diabetes, heart disease and HIV. Their medical expert described fundamental health-care systems as “deeply flawed,” while the filing alleges one preventable death from bleeding and sepsis. It also says more than a dozen people contracted measles in February and March 2026 and that a May ICE review found 16 percent of records examined lacked appropriate tuberculosis screening before placement in the general population. Detainees describe spending as much as 23 or 24 hours a day in windowless tent enclosures holding up to 72 people, amid dust, overflowing toilets, and inadequate hygiene supplies, with some reporting going days or weeks without outdoor recreation. A Newsweek investigation previously found that women detained at Camp East Montana described living in windowless tent enclosures amid overflowing toilets, mold and shortages of basic hygiene supplies, with some reporting limited medical care and days without access to the outdoors. Several also alleged verbal harassment by guards and obstacles to confidential communication with attorneys. Rita Lomio, senior counsel at the ACLU’s National Prison Project, said in a statement, “While litigation continues, a preliminary injunction is needed to end the most egregious abuses before more people needlessly suffer and die.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here . Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Cannon , James Debens , Gray R. item.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy [Reuters] A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating. But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel". The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look". It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law". In Saturday's incident the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah. They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest. Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown. The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle. Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice. "Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said. "As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. "Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them." Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved. But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security." The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters." "According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added. Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux, the left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries [Reuters] But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack. It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility". A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible." It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge". Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence. The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground. "It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged." "The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said. item.title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as hundreds arrested in France protests
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living. At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets. In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds. Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse. Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported. La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fire [Getty Images] Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving". However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République. Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups. Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons. A car was set alight at the Place de la République in Paris [Reuters] In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building". Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze. Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse. Limoges town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze, the prefecture said [Getty Images] A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened." The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers. Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence. Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied. Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers. Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris [Reuters] Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds. On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups. These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history. While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty. French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party. The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson. Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on Saturday [Getty Images] Watch: 'The mood has really shifted' at the Paris student protests Prime Minister Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical". He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence." Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence. Police fired water cannon at protesters in the Place de la République, Paris [Reuters] French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished." The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October. However, the protests have continued and intensified. Watch: 'Mood has really shifted' as Paris protesters clash with police Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election? item.title: GOP lawmakers criticize Trump's decision to waive Russia sanctions: 'Unconscionable'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Several GOP lawmakers criticized President Trump’s move to exempt Russia from the sanctions bill he signed law last month, with Sen. Thom Tillis (R- N.C.) calling the move "beyond irresponsible." Trump signed an executive order Friday evening to waive sanctions against Russia in a legislative package that was meant to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its military operations against Ukraine. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand? It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day,” Tillis wrote on the social platform X. The legislation, signed by Trump in September , would impose tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian energy, or on countries helping Russia evade sanctions. The sanctions bill was drafted by and named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). The late senator had announced a breakthrough on the legislation shortly before his death in July, saying lawmakers reached a deal with the White House to move it forward. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) posted the news on social media Saturday morning saying, “Lindsey would be appalled.” “The President is prolonging the war, not ending it,” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on social media , referring to Friday’s executive order. In his Friday order , the president noted that the legislation allows him to “waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person.” “I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.” In a post on social platform X Saturday, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) showed support for the president’s decision, calling the sanctions legislation “short-sighted.” He noted in his post that he was among only seven Republicans who voted against the bill. “Glad to see Trump has used the executive authority granted to him by Congress to waive almost all of the provisions of this stupid law that pertain to Russia,” Massie wrote. One the other side of the aisle, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who played a major role in passing the sanctions bill, called the president’s move to waive sanctions for Russia, a “craven, cowardly action.” “These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal wrote in his post. Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) also slammed the president’s move on social platform X , saying it “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.” The move comes after the president struck a deal with Russia last week permitting the country to sell diesel products to the U.S. and in the world market amid global fuel shortages. The deal prompted backlash from lawmakers across the board. In an interview with Piers Morgan, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he felt “betrayed” by the president’s decision. Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), who was among five House Republicans who signed a letter to the president urging him to cancel the Russia diesel deal, posted to X Saturday asking the president to “reverse course” on the sanction waivers. “Time and again, we have seen how Putin responds to American concessions: with contempt for the United States and increased violence against innocent Ukrainians,” McCaul wrote. item.title: Ukraine faces grim question of whether it can take on Russia with less U.S. backing
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The disruptions this week in U.S. support for Ukraine have forced Kyiv to face a grim question: Can it stay in the fight against Russia without any of President Trump’s already diminished support? Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has escalated a diplomatic assault, earlier this week accusing the Trump administration of throttling its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite services and failing to offer standard intelligence on incoming Russian strikes. So far, U.S. weapons seem to still be flowing to Europe despite Trump’s turns in the war. Uncertainty continues to swirl around who chose to limit SpaceX’s Starshield function, which has since been restored, but Reuters reported Thursday that the order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House. Leaders at the Defense Department reportedly were told that the service needed to be slowed. Then on Friday, Trump said that neither he nor Musk caused the Starlink outage , telling reporters: “I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all.” The episode highlights a growing rift between the U.S. and Ukraine, a dispute that puts Kyiv in danger and all but makes sure its war with Russia will stretch on for the foreseeable future, according to Branislav Slantchev, a political science professor at the University of California, San Diego. “This hurts Ukraine in more ways than just limiting its ability to operate on the frontlines,” Slantchev said. He placed the blame squarely on the Pentagon for disrupting Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield satellite services, with the former used for defensive purposes on the battlefield and the latter used for offensive operations. Starshield is controlled by the U.S. government and was slowed on Tuesday. He said the episode encourages Moscow to keep pushing with its demands including major territory concessions from Ukraine, as Russian President Vladimir Putin “estimates that the U.S. under Trump is on his side.” “Essentially, this guarantees that the war will continue,” Slantchev told The Hill. “Ukraine is not going to lose the war because of limited Starshield connectivity, but it makes Ukraine's task of incapacitating Russia's ability to hurt it much, much harder.” Relations between Washington and Kyiv, already strained since Trump began his second term last year, were pushed to a new low last week after he announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian oil sales. The agreement allows diesel to enter the U.S. and global marketplace, giving Moscow a lifeline as it struggles to make gains on the battlefield. Trump’s decision to allow the sales appeared influenced by the high cost of diesel in the United States, which has become an issue in congressional races, particularly in the Midwest. Yet there are doubts among experts of whether the step will reduce diesel’s costs given the connection between the high prices and turbulence in the Straight of Hormuz. Zelensky has spoken out against the deal, saying he feels betrayed, criticism that Trump met with threats to cut off U.S. intelligence sharing. Trump also demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries, saying Zelensky should be replaced as president. Trump has argued the Ukrainian attacks on the Russian infrastructure have contributed to rising fuel prices. Washington insists it had not stopped intelligence sharing, but that was called into doubt on Tuesday after Ukraine noted the disruption in Starlink service after the country reportedly was not alerted by allies ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv. The U.S. for more than four years has provided significant satellite and communications intelligence to Kyiv. Zelensky’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov, said that SpaceX without warning had introduced speed limits on its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, which “led to the failure of a number of missions.” “It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he said on Telegram. Zelensky then said Wednesday that the slowdown of Starlink was a “big mistake” and warned that Ukrainians could die if speeds were not restored. The Ukrainian leader also said that the U.S. is not “on the right side of history. Trump until Friday had remained quiet on the mystery surrounding the Starlink service. Musk has said Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government, deflecting any involvement. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said in a post to X on Wednesday, referring to Trump. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.” Musk, who provided Starlink to Ukraine shortly after Russia invaded the country in February 2022, has turned off the satellite internet service in the past. In September 2022, as Ukraine was attempting to retake territory from Russia, Musk reportedly gave an order to turn off Starlink, putting Ukrainian troops in a communications blackout. On Thursday the gloves seemed to come off for Kyiv after it reportedly said that it conducted a strike overnight against a Russian oil refinery. Prior to that, Ukraine had said it would hold off on striking Kremlin energy targets at Trump’s request. But Moscow did not make a similar agreement and has continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of a brutally cold and dark winter. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: The online campaign to share the Cornell rape accuser's identity reached millions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As a rape investigation at Cornell University spiraled into a national firestorm, some people went online to seek the identity of the alleged victim. Social media posts on X that attempted to reveal the name of the woman at the center of the case, identified in court filings only as Jane Doe, were viewed more than 87 million times over two weeks, according to data reviewed by The Washington Post. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Facebook, Instagram and TikTok attempted to limit the spread of content purporting to identify Jane Doe. All three platforms blocked searches for an alleged name for Jane Doe, although they appeared to allow some posts containing that name to stay online. Things were different on X, the platform owned by Elon Musk. The service allowed searches for the alleged name for Jane Doe and the company's chatbot, Grok, also posted it in replies to users at least 300 times, according to data compiled by researchers at the Center for Countering Digital Harm. X posts claiming to name or identify Jane Doe received 87 million views in a two-week period after local prosecutors said on Sept. 28 that they would reopen the investigation, according to the researchers. "A responsible organization would start thinking … does this break our rules? If not, something's wrong with our rules and we need to fix them," said Imran Ahmed, the chief executive of the nonprofit, which was previously known as the Center for Countering Digital Hate. "The problem is that we have accepted a lazy untruth, which is that there is nothing we can do about these platforms, and we have no say in the way they behave," he said. X did not respond to a request for comment. The platform's privacy policy prohibits sharing some types of private information without consent, such as a person's home address. It lists others, including names and birthdates, as data that "we don't consider to be private." Since Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house party in 2024, she has been harassed by anonymous callers and subjected to doxing, where people attempt to reveal personal information online, according to her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. He has also said that police appeared at her parents' home with guns drawn after a false report of an ongoing murder, a tactic known as swatting. Doe's suit seeks damages from seven fraternity members and Cornell University, among others. Several young men who share names with those accused in the lawsuit have also been targeted by harassment. Giuffra has said that online users have claimed to identify at least three women as Jane Doe on social media. The online response has been so ferocious that the judge in the case ordered several key documents, including the initial complaint, to be sealed over concerns about doxing. On X, the platform's artificial intelligence chatbot Grok contributed to the flood of posts containing alleged information about Jane Doe. Grok, which can publicly reply to users of the platform, appeared to pick up the alleged name from the online chatter. In some cases Grok provided the purported name in response to questions about Jane Doe. In others, the chatbot declined to confirm user requests to verify Jane Doe's identity and noted that alleged information for her was from unverified online speculation. When some users asked Grok to confirm their speculation about a partially redacted version of Jane Doe's signature in court documents, the chatbot obliged. "Highly probable," Grok said of one guess. "High plausibility," it responded to another. Grok's public posts in response to X users have previously caused controversy and forced a reaction from the platform. After users prompted the chatbot to digitally edit photos of women and girls into sexualized content, X said it had limited the feature. The first traces of X posts attempting to identify Jane Doe appeared on Sept. 29, the nonprofit's researchers said - the day after New York state prosecutors announced that they would reopen their investigation into the alleged rape. The posts peaked around the weekend of Oct. 3. Over the course of 10 days, more than 2,700 distinct users posted, nearly 90 percent of them with five posts or fewer. Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said its policies do not allow content that reveals the identity of people in legal cases where that has been restricted from public disclosure. TikTok did not have a comment. Limiting the search of a specific phrase - as TikTok, Instagram and Facebook did for an alleged name of Jane Doe - doesn't prevent potentially harmful content circulating. Users still get the vast majority of their content from their algorithmic feeds, said Laura Edelson, a professor at Northeastern University. A search block creates an "endless cat-and-mouse game," said Katherine Cross, a PhD candidate and lecturer at the University of Washington Information School. Users could easily get around the restrictions by substituting other characters in for letters, or swapping the order of keywords, she said. Platforms should also take down problematic posts, Cross said in an email. "The harm is already being done, and there is something profoundly inadequate and tokenistic about the search block," she said. "It is, doubtlessly, dissuading some people but it's a Band-Aid on a sucking wound." - - - Graphics: Posts on X spread speculation about Jane Doe's identity Posts purporting to name Jane Doe surged on X Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/online-campaign-unmask-cornell-rape-090000333.html

item.title: Online forum controlled by Nevada GOP House candidate contains slurs and Nazi talk
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Long before running for Congress , Marty O’Donnell was an award-winning music composer for the popular “Halo” video game franchise. His work drew legions of fans to an online forum, which the Nevada Republican has tried to turn into a galvanizing force as he tries to unseat a Democrat in a Las Vegas area district that could help decide House control . O’Donnell has served as the group’s de facto leader, referring to himself as its “benevolent dictator” while tapping its members for campaign cash and harnessing their enthusiasm in his bid. The campaign held a two-day event for forum members this month at a casino that included a video game tournament, panel discussions and speeches. There is another side, however, to what is known as “The Marty Army.” An Associated Press review of thousands of posts made on the forum between 2022 and 2026 found racial slurs, minimizations of Nazi Germany and defenses of white nationalist conspiracy theories. “It wasn’t a couple of crazies. The popular sentiment was, ‘Yes, slavery should be legal,’” said Deacon Dameron, a former group member who said O’Donnell banned him for calling another user a “dork.” Many views espoused in the forum, which is controlled by O’Donnell and his handpicked moderators, are at odds with some of the values articulated by the candidate and his campaign. For example, O’Donnell has staunchly defended Israel and condemned bigotry. In a statement, campaign spokesman Keith Schipper said O’Donnell “has zero tolerance for hate" in his forum. Since becoming aware of the issue in the spring, the campaign “dedicated a staffer to monitor” and “remove people that spew racist and antisemitic vitriol,” Schipper said. “Unfortunately, some posts have been missed over the years.” Schipper said nearly 200 users have been banned “because of hateful rhetoric, including many of the people flagged by the Associated Press. Marty’s support of Israel is unequivocal and, as seen in various interviews and online posts, he will not tolerate the rise of antisemitism in our country. Marty will continue to fight bigotry, misinformation, and hate toward Israel because it is the right and moral thing to do.” O’Donnell, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump, is running against four-term Rep. Susie Lee in the Nov. 3 election as Republicans look to hang onto their razor-thin majority. In a sign of how Republicans are triaging their chances in a tough environment, they pulled back spending this week in a handful of congressional races, including O’Donnell’s. From ‘Halo’ to emoji slurs Most of the chat group’s comments concern video games and gaming strategies. A section is reserved for questions about O’Donnell’s work on “Halo” games. After O’Donnell announced his first run for Congress in 2024, when he finished fourth in the party primary, some discussions centered around news and policy. Many of the offensive and controversial remarks came in freewheeling replies to otherwise anodyne comments about current events, politics or games. In May 2022, for example, a member wrote, “WE STAND WITH MARTY.” Others reacted to the post using letter emoji to spell out — incorrectly — a racial slur for Black people. More soon chimed in, using emoji letters to invoke another anti-Black slur. Users were likely restricted from properly spelling out such words because, by design, the platform prevents emoji from being used more than once in reaction to a post. During a January 2025 discussion concerning free speech, a forum member expressed a desire to use a racial slur but refrained because “that’s not the attention Marty wants.” Dameron, the former group member, and another former user said posters relied on coded language because more overt racist comments were likely to draw scrutiny from moderators. The other user spoke on condition of anonymity over fears of retaliation. “The Marty Army” began as a fan forum “The Marty Army” began as an inside joke. Developers of “Halo” created the chat room in 2001 on a website devoted to the game. The name they chose was meant to invoke a club for rabid fans of the glam rock band Kiss. O’Donnell joined the chat group and assumed control of the forum. He relocated it to Discord, a popular online platform. His candidate website contains a link to the Discord chat group, which he has also publicized from his account on the social media platform X. “Hey all! If you’d like to be part of my run for Congress, you can be part of Marty’s Army,” O’Donnell said in an X post after he launched his 2024 campaign. O’Donnell has stated repeatedly that users who espouse racist or antisemitic views will be banned. He also threatened, at times, to delete posts. The AP found some users who espoused Nazi sympathies were kicked off the forum, but many of their posts remain. A user suggested in March 2024 that the Nazis “did some good things” that were “completely overshadowed by the terrible things they did.” Another that month asked, “Was Hitler really an evil guy?” “Like aside from the Holocaust,” the user added, “did he really even do anything wrong?” In February, a third member posted, “Heil Hitler.” O'Donnell said he wore a Mussolini mask Current and historical fascist figures have also drawn approval. O’Donnell wrote on the forum that he rejects fascism. But he also shared a photo of himself wearing what he said was a mask of Benito Mussolini, the Italian dictator and key Hitler ally, that he wore to a Halloween party. O'Donnell's campaign denied he dressed up as Mussolini. “This mask was part of a scary Halloween costume nearly two decades ago. It was not labeled a Mussolini mask when he bought it nor was he dressed up as Mussolini for the holiday,” Schipper said. “He purchased it because it was the ugliest, creepy mask on the shelf. He jokingly referred to it as a ‘Mussolini mask’ years later because he realized it vaguely looked like Mussolini.” O’Donnell stated this year that he had been unaware of the resurgence of antisemitism. He told a conservative news outlet in September that he thought “that antisemitism is something we don’t have to worry about anymore.” “I guess it just went under the surface and it has been percolating there,” he added in the interview with the Washington Reporter, which was founded by Republican political strategists. O’Donnell made the comment after the news site Jewish Insider reported that he hosted Charles Cornish-Dale, a far-right influencer with Nazi sympathies, on his own podcast, “The Marty O’Donnell Show.” O’Donnell pledged to ban those who espouse antisemitism In the spring, O’Donnell warned users on the forum that if there was “even a hint of antisemitism” the offending member would be “instantly banned.” Users responded to his post with an emoji of an exaggerated nose and “GOY,” a sometimes disparaging Yiddish term for non-Jews. Some anti-hate groups view the use of the nose emoji as antisemitic, while goy is a term that has been appropriated by those who espouse antisemitic views. Wendy Melillo, an associate professor of journalism at American University who researches extremist chat rooms, said such comments were clearly “coded antisemitic hate speech.” Melillo said other posts she reviewed were more explicit. “There is nothing coded,” she said, “about ‘Heil Hitler.’” Some members of “The Marty Army” are aware the forum could pose a liability. In 2024, a user wrote that O’Donnell’s political career could face trouble “if someone does a vulnerability study and they find this server.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/online-forum-controlled-nevada-gop-123530042.html

item.title: Katie Zacharia praises Trump as ‘kind, wonderful, gracious’ after White House exit
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump's embattled new press secretary Katie Zacharia was forced out Friday after less than a week on the job. Zacharia confirmed widespread reports that Trump had let her go in a post on X just after 9 p.m. ET Friday, alongside a photo of the two of them in the Oval Office. “President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man,” she wrote. “I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him.” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung told CNN in a statement that Zacharia "will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role." Zacharia is the shortest-tenured White House press secretary in U.S. history. Her five days on the job fell well short of Anthony Scaramucci’s 11 days as Trump’s communications director in 2017. Trump is unlikely to name a new press secretary anytime soon, two sources familiar with his thinking told NBC News . Earlier Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia was on her way out, telling reporters that he had asked Zacharia to "reconsider" whether she "need[s] this." "I told her, 'I think you're better off being happy and I don't think you could ever be happy in this job,'" Trump said. Asked if he was planning to "fire" Zacharia, the president said no. But, he added, "I want her to have a good life. I don't want [her] to have a life like she's led in the last three days. She is being brutalized by the media." Around the same time, multiple outlets reported that Zacharia had already been let go. Citing "three people familiar with the matter," the New York Times reported on Friday afternoon that Trump had "fired" Zacharia. A senior White House official told Fox News that Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role, and CBS News, Politico and the Washington Post published similar reports. Zacharia was in the middle of an interview with the Wall Street Journal at her West Wing desk shortly before 1 p.m. Friday when she was called away, the Journal reported . She had just told the reporters, “There are no staffing changes that are happening.” Senior Trump adviser Jason Miller then knocked on her door and said Vice President JD Vance wanted to talk. “JD wanted to chat with us real quick,” Miller said, according to the Journal. Zacharia left and never returned to the interview. Trump: "I told Katie that in my opinion she was treated very very unfairly by the news. Let's call it the fake news. I said, 'Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this.' We're talking about doing something. I want her to have a good life. She's being brutalized by the… pic.twitter.com/Ivkk5imCjS — Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 16, 2026 The president announced on Friday, Oct. 9, that he had chosen Zacharia, a conservative commentator and former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration in August. Zacharia started at the White House on Monday and gave her first press briefing on Tuesday. But she has spent the days since then facing questions about her own legal credentials rather than Trump's agenda. In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump described Zacharia as an "attorney" as well as "a devoted fan and member of MAGA!" Zacharia holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, and her LinkedIn page says she served as "general counsel" at Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former acting Kennedy Center director Ric Grenell to promote conservative policies in the Golden State. In media appearances, Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that while Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school, she "didn't pass." A senior administration official confirmed to NBC News that Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam. Reuters also investigated her credentials and "could not find records showing Zacharia was registered as an attorney or member of the bar in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia." Asked by reporters Tuesday on the South Lawn where she passed the bar, Zacharia twice replied, "When I moved to China." In a phone interview with the New York Times on Wednesday , Zacharia said she misheard the question. "I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she told the paper. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One. And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question." Zacharia pointed out that it was only her second day on the job. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia looks on as President Trump speaks to reporters on the South Lawn on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson In a statement to the Washington Post , the White House said that "Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law." According to USA Today , Zacharia "worked for a Chinese law firm's international-practice team on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements involving investments through the World Bank." She did not attempt to take the bar exam a second time. On Thursday, Zacharia confirmed that she did not pass the bar, telling the conservative outlet Real America's Voice that she was "incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited" at the time by her impending marriage and move to China. "We just said… 'I'll take the bar and see what happens,'" Zacharia recalled. "The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China." On Wednesday, a nonprofit watchdog group called Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California bar asking it to investigate whether Zacharia had violated state law by "repeatedly holding herself out as a lawyer." White House spokesperson Steven Cheung responded on social media by dismissing the Campaign for Accountability as a "radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." Legal experts told the Times that it's debatable whether a law school graduate can describe herself as a "lawyer" before she passes the bar. But she cannot call herself an "attorney" — someone who is licensed to practice law and give legal advice — nor can she serve as a "general counsel" or as an "associate" at a Chinese law firm, they added. Zacharia told Real America's Voice that she was "very careful about how I executed this and I never came across as somebody who was an attorney-at-law." "I consulted for a very long time many people in the field — 'Is it OK and acceptable if I label myself 'lawyer' … and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," she explained. "They said, 'Absolutely,' across the board. 'You can call yourself a lawyer.'" On Thursday night, Fox News host Sean Hannity pressed Zacharia on her halting explanation . "Why not just say, 'I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. "Why get into this long drawn-out thing about the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?" "When I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar," Zacharia said. "I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law." Hours before she was forced out, Zacharia told “Fox & Friends” on Friday that no one had asked whether she passed the bar before she was hired. “Those questions weren’t asked,” she said. “I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel,” according to The Hill . What happened in Zacharia's first briefing? White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the Briefing Room on Oct. 13. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Zacharia's first briefing lasted 15 minutes, most of which was taken up by her opening statement. "I am so honored to work for President Trump and the American people as the new White House press secretary," Zacharia told reporters in the Briefing Room. "I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work with him for a very long time." She took questions from three news outlets — Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail — before ending the briefing. Asked what she planned to do as press secretary, Zacharia said, "I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was getting to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda for the American people." In his post on Truth Social announcing her appointment, Trump said Zacharia "has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning." Zacharia called the appointment "the honor of a lifetime" in a post on X . Who is Katie Zacharia? President Donald Trump and Katie Zacharia. Katie Zacharia/X The 42-year-old California native and mother of four left her role as senior communications adviser to Trump Media and Technology Group, which runs Truth Social, to join the White House. Before that, she served for about two months as a deputy assistant secretary and spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to her LinkedIn profile . She was best known for her frequent appearances defending the administration's policies on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News and other outlets. She told CNN in April — around the time she left DHS — that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol." Zacharia first came to Washington in 2006 to intern for the Republican National Committee while George W. Bush was president. She lives in California with her husband and their four young children. During Tuesday's briefing, she was asked about juggling the competing roles of being a mother and White House press secretary. "The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable," Zacharia said, before confusing her spouse with her boss. "So my president — excuse me, my husband — is out here." Zacharia then praised Trump as the "most family-friendly president we've ever had" and said her family will be moving from California to Washington, D.C., soon. CNN reported on Friday that Zacharia's "selection came about quickly" and that she "was not being considered for the role" as of "last week." CNN also reported that "on multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list" of possible press secretaries "only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position." In a New York Post column in February , Zacharia recounted a clash with liberal patrons of her "local cardio kickboxing gym" that ended with the gym owner asking her not to wear her red "Team Trump 2024" hat to exercise class. "I responded that I would never take my Trump hat off to appease the left," Zacharia wrote. "I refuse to stay silent." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/article/katie-zacharia-out-as-white-house-press-secretary-after-5-days-on-the-job-reports-182158704.html

item.title: Dad crawled through broken window to stop gunman at daughters' school, family says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The bystander who stepped in to stop a gunman at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, has come forward and identified himself as Kaylub Giamanco, a lifelong Bend resident who has two daughters at the school . At a news conference Friday, police also praised a teacher who threw a cellphone at the gunman, tackled him and fought to take his weapon. Police said Giamanco pursued and fatally shot the 16-year-old attacker, ending a rampage that took the lives of three children and a teacher and wounded two others. A statement released by Giamanco's family on Friday said, "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support." "The tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary has devastated the Bend community," they wrote. Giamanco and his family asked for privacy and said they will not be giving interviews. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz credited him and a teacher at the school for actions that saved other lives. "In addition to the 36-year-old man who bravely stepped in to stop the suspect, I want to highlight another person whose heroic action we need to recognize: a teacher in the classroom threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him. She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," he said. President Trump on Friday called the Giamanco a "great hero" who "took care of business." "Thank God we had him; otherwise, it would have been much worse," Mr. Trump said, adding: "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it." Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek also praised the bystander who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life," saying the person's actions carry "a heavy emotional burden." Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, says he called her shortly after it happened. "Kaylub knew something was not right, so he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school," she said in an exclusive interview with CBS News Sacramento . "He crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army-crawled through the window." She says he told her: "'A man went into my daughter's school and shot kids,' and he said, 'and I looked at him point-blank, and I shot and killed him, Mom.'" "I told him he was a hero, he did what he had to do, and that he did the right thing, and that I was proud of him and that he was a hero and he saved a lot of lives," she said. "And he said, 'Mom, I couldn't save them all.' " Freeman said, "Kaylub has a genuine heart and he loves his community and his family and his children," adding, "He's just a good person, in general." When police arrived minutes later, Krantz says they found the deceased shooter and four victims — three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher — inside the school. Two other victims, a student and a teacher, were hospitalized with critical injuries. At Friday's briefing, Krantz said the gunman has been identified as Griffin J. John II. He used a shotgun purchased by his mother, law enforcement sources told CBS News. The suspect was from Bend and had previously attended the school, police said. This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/oregon-school-shooter-bystander-identified-silver-rail-elementary/

item.title: Proposed bill could be the break Hollywood has been waiting for
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The beleaguered U.S. film and TV industry, which has seen significant dollars leave for foreign countries, local production plummet and thousands of jobs vanish, may have some relief on the way. It comes in the form of proposed legislation that has the rare support of lawmakers across the political spectrum. Indeed, President Donald Trump and the actors union SAG-AFTRA have been equally vocal in throwing their weight behind the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, which aims to create a significant tax incentive to bring Hollywood back home. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The bill was introduced in Congress in late September and is now with the House Ways and Means Committee. Given the bipartisan support, it is likely to have a relative glide path on Capitol Hill. “Both parties represent people who work on sets, run catering companies and own hotels,” said Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas), who co-wrote the bill. “Co-sponsors come from California, Georgia, New York, Ohio and Tennessee, and every one of us has heard the same thing at home: The work is going overseas.” For film and TV creatives and craftspeople, the bill can’t land on the White House’s Resolute Desk a moment too soon. “Whatever you think about the current administration, at least Trump, if he puts his weight behind this, could actually make this really move quickly, which is what we need,” said Carolina Groppa, an Emmy-nominated producer who also hosts a podcast, “Angle on Producers,” about the industry. “The patient’s been on the gurney for a long time, collectively across the United States.” Film and TV production has indeed been fleeing Los Angeles for years - and often leaving the U.S. entirely. Other countries, from Ireland and Canada to Serbia and Colombia, have introduced huge tax incentives that have enticed producers to move projects to wherever is best for the bottom line. According to a recent report from EY Quantitative Economics and Statistics, the share of production spending for studio films with primarily U.S.-based projects declined since the turn of the century from 74 percent to 42 percent; for TV, it fell from 94 percent to 64 percent. That trend accelerated following the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild of America strikes, which were themselves triggered in part by industry contraction following the pandemic. “You could just feel the town change,” said Elsbeth Mumm, a set decorator based in Los Angeles. “Shows were being canceled, movies were getting pushed, scripts were just disappearing, things that had gotten green-lit were just stopped.” The people who have been hurt most are the middle class of the entertainment industry: the writers, production staff and craftspeople who often live project to project. When filmmaking fled overseas, many of their lives changed. “People are losing houses,” Mumm said. “People have lost their health care. People have lost their retirement.” The federal program would give certain film and TV productions a 20 percent tax rebate. To qualify, they would have to cost over $1 million, with at least 75 percent of the principal photography days occurring domestically. The bill would allow the federal rebate to be stacked on top of existing state incentives. “If what is in the bill goes through and is executed as promised, it will be a massive game changer,” said Patrick Meaney, an independent film director. “I think people are almost underrating it or not really processing it because it came out of nowhere and seems too good to be true.” The tax incentive structure is somewhat similar to a smaller plan in effect in California, which last year was significantly broadened to include up to $750 million in credits annually. Many in Hollywood feel the program’s expansion has been a success. The outlook is hopeful “for the first time in a long time,” said Keith Raskin, a veteran producer currently working on a crime comedy, “Sunset P.I.,” which is set to premiere on NBC in 2027. He’s filming in Los Angeles thanks to the state tax rebate program. “When I make phone calls to crew members to hire them, they cry because it means that they can make a payment on their house or they can keep their insurance for another year.” If the federal rebate passes, it would mean “we’re finally a player in the world market,” Raskin added. One big difference from the California credit: The federal version is uncapped. Despite its bipartisan support, some critics argue that the tax incentives would first and foremost benefit the richest players in the system - massive entities like Paramount Skydance and the star actors and directors who are their top moneymakers. “Do we really need kickbacks to corporations to employ a whole labor force?” asked Andi Brittan, a veteran set decorator and union leader at the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees Local 44. “Unfortunately, the truth is, we have to work within the system, and working within the system means supporting these kinds of tax incentives.” Other detractors point to past economic reports showing that these kinds of tax subsidies provide little to no quantifiable value. For example, a 2023 report published by the state of New York found that from 2012 to 2022, the tax incentives didn’t generate as many jobs as would have been created in other industries. Still, the report also noted there are probably indirect positive economic effects that are hard to quantify. That’s something many in the industry focus on. “It’s not just the films,” Mumm said. “It’s the trickling out - the florists, the food stylists, all of this stuff outside of the industry that rely on this huge force purchasing from them.” It may be too late to ever fully recover from years of being beat on production costs, and there’s still major concern about the impact of the Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. Even so, the rank and file of the U.S. film industry are uttering words like “optimistic.” “I feel a good amount of hope, and I’ll tell you why,” said Kevin Armento, a film and TV writer. “All those soundstages are still sitting there. They haven’t bulldozed them yet.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/17/tax-breaks-tinseltown-would-aim-keep-film-tv-production-us/

item.title: 2 people killed, including 6-year-old boy, after mother drives into soccer game: Police
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Two people, including a 6-year-old boy, were killed and 11 others injured after a truck drove through a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday afternoon, police said, in what officials called a "heartbreaking" incident that authorities are still investigating. First responders rushed to Stryker Soccer Complex after receiving multiple 911 calls around 3:25 p.m. CT, Capt. Aaron Moses of the Wichita Police Department told reporters at a press conference Saturday evening. KAKE - PHOTO: In this image taken from a video, police respond to the scene at the Stryker Sports Complex. Police said the driver, who they identified only as a 34-year-old woman of Garden City, Kansas, stayed with the truck after the incident. "She has been cooperative to this point in the investigation," he said, adding later she was in police custody. Moses told reporters he believed one of the driver's children was playing soccer at the complex on Saturday but was not on that field at the time of the incident. KAKE - PHOTO: First responders are shown at the scene of an incident at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Oct. 17, 2026. There were two juveniles who were also inside the truck at the time it went onto the field, police said. The 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man, both of McPherson, Kansas, were pronounced dead on the scene, police said. Of the 11 people who were injured, five are children, ranging in age from 5 to 9. Wichita Police Department - PHOTO: In this screen grab from a video posted to social media, Captain Aaron Moses of the Wichita Police Department speaks to the media on Oct. 17, 2026, in Wichita, Kansas. The injured adults range in age from 28 to 68. Of the injured, 10 had "traumatic injuries," Moses said, saying they ranged from bruises to "extremely severe injuries." Police stressed they are still investigating and asked the public for patience. "We know what happened, but now we're working very hard to find out why it happened, and we're not there yet," Wichita Police Chief Joe Sullivan told reporters. Police said they have interviewed over 30 witnesses at the scene and are asking anyone with pictures or video of the incident to share them with investigators. Police also credited bystanders who the police chief said "sprang into action so quickly and gave life-saving assistance until the arrival of first responders." Sullivan added, "It was truly amazing, but I think it's indicative of the of the Wichita community." Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said "Tonight, Wichita grieves together." "Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita," Mayor Lily Wu told reporters. "Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon watching their children play soccer. No one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold." The city of Wichita said in a Facebook post Saturday afternoon that all events at the sports complex have been canceled until further notice. KAKE - PHOTO: First responders are shown at the scene of an incident at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Oct. 17, 2026. "We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time," the city said in a statement. Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly said in a statement she was monitoring the situation and in touch with the mayor. KAKE - PHOTO: First responders are shown at the scene of an incident at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas, on Oct. 17, 2026.
